newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ sees scope for further NZ easing in Dec.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ sees scope for further NZ easing in Dec.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand said on Friday there may be some scope for a further small easing in monetary conditions in the December quarter.
However, the RBNZ said in its six monthly Monetary Policy Statement the market had already pushed conditions far enough in the meantime and it was not seeking any further easing.
Despite that signal, the market rallied heartily on the statement, taking conditions a further 40 basis points (in interest rate terms) below the RBNZ's new assumptions.
The bank's MPS assumed conditions would be the equivalent of 100 basis points easier during the September quarter than the conditions assumed in the March economic projections.
"This new level of desired monetary conditions is in fact very close to where actual monetary conditions have been in recent weeks," RBNZ Governor Don Brash explained.
"In other words, we are not seeking any further easing in actual monetary conditions."
But the RBNZ's nominal Monetary Conditions Index, which the bank wanted to average 825 over the September quarter, fell from that level to 784.8 half an hour after the statement.
A 100 point move in the MCI is the same as a 100 basis point move in short rates or a two percent change in the currency's Trade-Weighted Index.
Dealers said the easing was at the extreme end of market expectations and had been greeted with glee.
"We were a little surprised they've sanctioned so much easing at this point in time," said Paul Stewart, chief economist at ANZ Bank.
Explaining its easing, the RBNZ said indicators suggested there was quite an abrupt slowing during the first three months of the year which the bank had not expected.
"Indeed, it is not inconceivable that the economy may even have contracted slightly in that quarter," Brash said.
However, June quarter indicators suggested the economy may have rebounded somewhat, and the RBNZ saw growth strengthening in subsequent quarters.

Beyond 1997, the bank saw the need for monetary conditions to remain reasonably firm. The economy would not have much extra capacity available by mid-1998, when further tax cuts and increased government spending would take effect, it said.
